collection.description: Up in the hills, two springs bubble out of the rock side by side, a hand's width apart.

ask.text:
Up in the hills, two springs bubble out of the rock side by side, a hand's width apart. One is sweet, the elders say, and one is sour, and nobody remembers which is which, because whoever drinks from the sour one forgets. The sweet one, they say, makes a person content with what they have. The sour one takes away something they love.
(Name) is very thirsty after a long climb. Both springs look exactly the same. Should (name) drink from the left one, or the right?

c1o1.text: By the time (name) gets home, the taste of stone has faded, and so has something else. When (his/her) friends go down to the lagoon that afternoon, (name) doesn't go with them, and can't think why (he/she) ever wanted to. Swimming, which (he/she) loved more than anything, just seems wet. (He/She) doesn't remember which spring (he/she) drank from.

c1o2.text: The water tastes of stone, and then, very faintly, of honey. On the walk home, (name) finds (himself/herself) humming. The next morning (he/she) gets up and goes to work without the usual groan, and the morning after, and finds the work isn't the weight it used to be. "The left one," (he/she) tells everyone. "Remember. The left one's sweet."

c1.text: (Name) kneels at the left spring, cups (his/her) hands, and drinks deeply. The water is cold and tastes of stone...

c2o1.text: It tastes lovely. That's the trick, it turns out. At the festival that evening, when the drums start, (name) stays sitting down. (He/She) used to be first up to dance, and now (he/she) just doesn't feel like it, and can't remember ever having felt like it. (He/She) doesn't remember which spring (he/she) drank from either.

c2o2.text: The water is sweet all the way down, and (name) remembers exactly which spring it was. On the way home, (he/she) passes the meeting hut, where a noisy crowd is gathered for the evening, and instead of slipping past as usual, (he/she) goes in and sits down in the middle of it all. (He/She) used to hate crowds. Now, it seems, (he/she) doesn't.

c2.text: (Name) kneels at the right spring, cups (his/her) hands, and drinks. The water is warm and tastes faintly of flowers...
